CLUBS LESSON · EXTRA-CURRICULAR ACTIVITIES · AGES 3–12 YEARS

Astronomy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts the astronomy club habit: a moon diary that fills in shape by shape, one bright planet found together, and the big-question hour where wonder does the teaching.

What is this?

Astronomy club is regular sky time — moon watching, star finding, question nights — where the printed skills are Wonder & Discovery: the big questions and the patient looking that answers them. It is the club that meets after bedtime and still gets permission.

What does it mean?

The moon diary teaches the deepest sky fact: the sky changes on schedule, and anyone can learn the schedule. Finding one planet teaches scale gently — that light traveled minutes or years to reach the eyes.

What does the child need to know?

A small notebook for the moon diary, a clear evening or two a week, a red flashlight (red keeps night eyes ready) if possible, and one star map or app. A window works; outdoors works better.

Why this matters

Astronomy builds observation over time, scale thinking and the honest habit of checking — is the moon really the same shape? It also seeds the physics questions every curious child eventually asks, with the sky already familiar ground.

What it teaches

Pattern observation across nights, recording discipline (dated drawings), scale and distance intuition, question-asking courage, and the patience of slow change.

Words to learn

moonphasecrescentplanetstartelescopeorbitskynight

Say this to your child

“"Astronomy club meets tonight! Bring the diary — first we guess tonight’s moon, then we look. Planets hold still, stars twinkle: which is that bright one? And every night ends with one question for next time."”

Step by step

  1. Start the moon diary: same notebook, same pencil, one dated drawing per clear night — shape and where it sat in the sky.
  2. Week two: the child predicts tonight’s moon shape BEFORE looking — astronomers guess, then check.
  3. Find one planet together: a steady bright light (planets hold still; stars twinkle) — Venus or Jupiter usually plays along.
  4. Star stories night: pick one constellation, learn its name and its story — the sky carried the library before books.
  5. The big-question hour: why does the moon change? what is a star? End every session with one question written down for next time — the club always leaves with homework from the sky.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the astronomer leans into a telescope on a tripod with one eye closed — the wink is half concentration and half delight, which is the honest face of discovery.

Ask your child

"What shape is tonight’s moon — and were we right?" "How do we tell a planet from a star?" (steady light vs twinkling) "What question did the sky give us tonight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child may guard the moon diary like a logbook, spot the moon in daylight (allowed — astronomers nod), or ask where the sun goes at night — which is the club’s favorite homework.

Out in the real world

Astronomers, satellite engineers and every navigation system in history run on sky patterns. The moon diary is a real observing log in miniature — dated drawings, honest checks.

Try it together

Backyard scale walk: if the sun were a soccer ball on the porch, the child walks the neighborhood model to find where Earth would sit — a marble about fifty meters away. Scale becomes walkable.

Understanding check

Ask: "Show me a crescent with your hands." "Why do we date the diary?" (the sky changes on schedule) "What twinkles — planet or star?" (star)

This lesson pairs with the Astronomy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Extra-Curricular Activities.
